problems: stop 2 card 13, answer 1: copies a Prep line word for word

explanations.explanation: The verse says the man and his family went to live in the land of Moab (Ruth 1:1). They left Bethlehem because of famine and settled in Moab for a time (Ruth 1:1–2).
The text does not say Egypt; it specifically names Moab as the place they moved (Ruth 1:1). Egypt was a common destination in other stories, but not this one.
Edom is not mentioned here. The family travels to Moab, not Edom, according to the verse (Ruth 1:1).
Ruth is the name given in the verse as one of the two Moabite wives (Ruth 1:4). The other is Orpah, and both marry Naomi’s sons in Moab (Ruth 1:4).
Rachel is a well-known Bible name, but she is not one of Naomi’s daughters-in-law here. The text names Orpah and Ruth as the wives (Ruth 1:4).
Dinah is a different Bible figure and is not named in this passage. The two Moabite women are Orpah and Ruth (Ruth 1:4).

The passage says that after about ten years in Moab, both Mahlon and Chilion died, leaving Naomi without her two sons (Ruth 1:5). That loss is the heart of Naomi’s grief in this section. The text gives that as the event, not any house fire or illness mentioned here.

explanations.answer: Her house in Moab burns down
explanations.explanation: The verse does not mention a fire. It records the deaths of Naomi’s two sons as the cause of her being left without them (Ruth 1:5).

explanations.answer: She falls sick and loses her sight
explanations.explanation: There is no mention of Naomi becoming sick or blind in these verses. The text focuses on the death of her husband and sons (Ruth 1:3, 5).
Naomi hears that the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food (Ruth 1:6). That news prompts her decision to return to Judah with her daughters-in-law (Ruth 1:6–7).
The verse does not say a king was provided. It speaks of the LORD providing food for His people, which is why Naomi heads back home (Ruth 1:6).
The text specifically mentions food being provided, not a military victory. Naomi’s choice to go home is tied to relief from famine (Ruth 1:6).

explanations.answer: Go back to their mothers' homes
explanations.explanation: Naomi tells Orpah and Ruth to 'go back, each of you to your mother’s home' (Ruth 1:8). She blesses them and urges them to find rest in a new husband’s home (Ruth 1:8–9).

explanations.answer: Walk faster to beat the dark
explanations.explanation: That detail is not in the passage. Naomi’s instruction is to return to their mothers’ homes, not a hurried walk (Ruth 1:8).

explanations.answer: Stay close to her the whole way
explanations.explanation: On the contrary, Naomi asks them to go back to their people and mothers’ homes (Ruth 1:8). She does not tell them to stay with her.

True — Naomi prays that the LORD would show them loving devotion and that each would find rest in the home of a new husband (Ruth 1:8–9). Her words are a blessing and a practical farewell for their futures.
False would be wrong here because the text does include Naomi’s blessing that they find rest in the homes of new husbands (Ruth 1:9). She is sending them back with a prayer for their well-being.

explanations.answer: We will return with you to your people
explanations.explanation: They tell Naomi they will return with her to her people (Ruth 1:10). Their words show devotion, even though Naomi later urges them to go back (Ruth 1:11–13).

explanations.answer: We will stay in Moab and wait for you
explanations.explanation: The women do not say they will stay in Moab; they say they will go with Naomi to her people (Ruth 1:10). Naomi responds by trying to send them back (Ruth 1:11–13).

explanations.answer: We will come visit you in Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: They promise to return with her to her people, not only a visit to Bethlehem (Ruth 1:10). The language shows a deeper commitment than a mere visit.

explanations.answer: Would you wait for them to grow up
explanations.explanation: Naomi asks whether they would wait for sons she might bear to grow up—she’s pointing out how unlikely it is and asking whether they would postpone their own futures (Ruth 1:13). The verse gives that as her reason to send them back (Ruth 1:11–13).

explanations.answer: Would you raise them as your own
explanations.explanation: That specific idea isn’t in her question. Naomi’s point is whether they would wait for hypothetical sons to grow up, not about raising children (Ruth 1:11–13).

explanations.answer: Would you go ahead to Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: She does not ask them to go ahead to Bethlehem; she urges them to return to their own families instead (Ruth 1:11–13).

explanations.answer: The LORD's hand has turned against her
explanations.explanation: Naomi says it is more bitter for her because 'the hand of the LORD has gone out against me' (Ruth 1:13). She understands her losses as part of the suffering she’s experiencing in God’s providence.

explanations.answer: The people of Judah have turned against her
explanations.explanation: The verse does not blame the people of Judah. Naomi speaks of the LORD’s hand being against her, not the people (Ruth 1:13).

explanations.answer: The people of Moab have turned against her
explanations.explanation: That is not what the text says. Naomi attributes her bitterness to the LORD’s hand against her, not to Moabites or others (Ruth 1:13).
True — the text says Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye (Ruth 1:14). Orpah returns to her people, while Ruth clings to Naomi (Ruth 1:14–15).
False would be incorrect here because the verse records Orpah kissing Naomi goodbye before she leaves (Ruth 1:14).
True is incorrect for this card — Ruth does not go back home with Orpah. The text says Orpah leaves, but Ruth clings to Naomi and refuses to go (Ruth 1:14–16).
False is correct — Ruth stays with Naomi instead of returning home with Orpah (Ruth 1:14–16). Ruth’s vow shows her determined loyalty (Ruth 1:16–17).

True — Naomi tells Ruth that Orpah has returned to her people and her gods and urges Ruth to follow her sister-in-law back (Ruth 1:15). Naomi wants what she thinks is best for them, to return to their families (Ruth 1:8, 15).
False would be wrong because the verse records Naomi telling Ruth to follow Orpah back to her people and her gods (Ruth 1:15). Naomi continues to push them toward their own families.

explanations.answer: Naomi's God will be her God
explanations.explanation: Ruth explicitly says, 'your people will be my people, and your God will be my God' (Ruth 1:16). That is central to her pledge to Naomi and marks her commitment beyond family ties.

explanations.answer: She will take care of Naomi's house
explanations.explanation: That detail is not part of Ruth’s declaration. Her promise focuses on following Naomi and adopting her people and God (Ruth 1:16).

explanations.answer: She will learn all the ways of Judah
explanations.explanation: Ruth does not say she will learn all Judah’s ways. Her vow is about personal allegiance: Naomi’s people and Naomi’s God become hers (Ruth 1:16).
Ruth says that only death should separate her and Naomi — she calls for severe punishment if anything else parts them (Ruth 1:17). The word expresses the absolute seriousness of her commitment.
The verse does not say 'distance'; it uses the stronger language of 'death' as the only thing that should separate them (Ruth 1:17).
Marriage is not what the text mentions as the only separating thing. Ruth vows that only death should separate her from Naomi (Ruth 1:17).

explanations.answer: She stops trying to persuade her
explanations.explanation: When Naomi sees Ruth’s determination, she stops trying to change her mind (Ruth 1:18). The text says Naomi 'stopped trying to persuade her,' showing Ruth’s resolve wins the moment.

explanations.answer: She sends her back after Orpah
explanations.explanation: Naomi does not send Ruth back after Orpah once Ruth makes her pledge; instead she accepts Ruth’s decision and stops persuading her (Ruth 1:18).

explanations.answer: She tells her to wait in Moab
explanations.explanation: The verse does not say Naomi tells Ruth to wait in Moab. Naomi stops persuading Ruth after seeing she is determined to go with her (Ruth 1:18).
The women of Bethlehem ask, 'Can this be Naomi?' when they see her return (Ruth 1:19). Her appearance and story have changed the town’s expectations.
The text records the women asking, 'Can this be Naomi?' rather than asking about Naomi’s husband (Ruth 1:19).
While Ruth may have seemed like a stranger to some, the verse specifically quotes the women saying, 'Can this be Naomi?' (Ruth 1:19).
Naomi tells them to call her Mara, meaning 'bitter,' because she feels the Almighty has dealt bitterly with her (Ruth 1:20). Her name change expresses her grief and sense of loss.
Hannah is not the name Naomi asks for; she says 'Call me Mara' because of her bitter experience (Ruth 1:20).
Leah is not the name Naomi chooses. The text records Naomi asking to be called Mara to reflect her bitterness (Ruth 1:20).
That statement is reversed from the text. Naomi says she 'went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty'—she returned empty, not full (Ruth 1:21).
False is correct — Naomi says she left full and returned empty, showing the losses she suffered (Ruth 1:21). Her words underline how bitter her experience has been.
The verse says they arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest (Ruth 1:22). That detail sets the scene for the next steps in the story.
The text names the barley harvest specifically, not wheat (Ruth 1:22). Barley harvest is the season mentioned here.
Olives are not referenced in this verse. The passage records their arrival at the start of the barley harvest (Ruth 1:22).
